collection.description: There is an old dance that only the elders know, slow and stamping, with clapping in odd places.

ask.text:
There is an old dance that only the elders know, slow and stamping, with clapping in odd places. It is called the Turning-Back Dance, and the story is that when it is danced right, by someone young leading the old ones, it turns back the years a little, for one night. Nobody has danced it right in a lifetime. The last person who knew the steps properly was (subject)'s great-grandmother.
Tonight is the full moon festival, and the elders have asked (subject) to lead it. (subject.He/She) has spent all week learning the steps from (elder), who remembers most of them, and argues with (subject.himself/herself) about the rest.
Should (subject) follow (elder)'s steps exactly, or dance it the way (subject.he/she) feels it?

c1o1.text: It works. As the drums stop, the elders standing round the fire look at each other and gasp. Every one of them has a young face: smooth cheeks, bright eyes, luscious hair. Their knees are still old. Their backs are still old. But their faces are the faces they had at twenty-five. They laugh, and point, and the oldest of them cries. (elder) is very smug about the steps.

c1o2.text: (elder) has one step wrong. The turn should have been to the left. Halfway through, the elders start crashing into each other, and the dance falls apart in a heap of old people and loud complaints. Only (elder), at the bottom of the heap, has had the years turned back, to a sprightly fifty. Everyone else has bruises. "It was LEFT," says (elder). "I see that now."

c1.text: (subject) leads the elders round the fire, stamping and clapping exactly as (elder) taught (subject.him/her). Stamp, stamp, turn, clap. The elders follow, slow at first, then faster, and the drums speed up to match...

c2o1.text: It isn't the Turning-Back Dance any more. It's something new. It doesn't turn back the elders' years. It does something to (subject), who comes out of it at dawn with a face younger than (subject.his/her) own, glowing. The whole village is happier for it. The elders make (subject) teach them the new steps, and call it (subject)'s Dance.

c2o2.text: Nothing turns back. But the elders dance until midnight, and the children join in, and then everyone does, round and round the fire. In the morning a lot of people can't walk properly, and nobody minds. (elder) says the old steps were better. Then (subject.he/she) asks (subject) to show (subject.him/her) the new ones again, slowly.

c2.text: (subject) starts with the old steps, then lets the drums carry (subject.him/her) somewhere else. The elders follow (subject.him/her), confused at first, then laughing, then dancing like nobody has seen them dance in years...
